q: What is memory, and how did Endel Tulving describe episodic memory?
a: Memory includes retaining, retrieving and using information about stimuli, images, events, ideas and skills after the original information is no longer present. A past experience can influence current or future behavior without being visible in the environment. Endel Tulving described episodic memory as a kind of mental time travel, because remembering an event connects it back to the experienced past.

q: What are encoding, storage and retrieval, and why does a failure to remember not tell you which one went wrong?
a: Encoding converts information into a form that can be stored, storage keeps it, and retrieval brings it back out when it is needed. Memory is an active system that can organize and even alter information, so it is not a recording that is kept unchanged. Because a failure to use information could come from a problem at any of the three operations, forgetting on its own does not show which one failed. Forgetting a familiar name could mean it was never encoded well, was lost from storage, or cannot be retrieved right now.

q: How is the memory tree organized, and where do episodic and semantic memory sit in it?
a: The tree splits memory into sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory. Long-term memory then splits into declarative memory, which contains episodic events and semantic knowledge, and procedural memory, which concerns skills. Declarative memory therefore has two branches, episodic memory and semantic memory. So episodic and semantic memory are branches of declarative memory inside long-term memory. They are not extra short-term stores, and the classification sorts memories by function rather than claiming all memories last equally long or hold the same kind of content.

q: What are the three stores of Atkinson and Shiffrin’s (1968) modal model, and what does each hold and for how long?
a: Sensory memory briefly retains incoming stimulation for seconds or fractions of a second. Short-term memory holds about five to seven items for roughly fifteen to twenty seconds. Long-term memory retains large amounts of information for years or even decades. Rehearsal is the control process that keeps information available in short-term memory and supports its transfer toward long-term memory.
note: The slides give short-term memory as five to seven items for about fifteen to twenty seconds. Modern work puts working capacity nearer three to four chunks, which matches the three to four items the slides give for visual short-term memory.

q: What happens at each stage from looking at a phone directory to dialing a number?
a: Looking at the directory floods sensory memory with many pieces of visual information at once, and it is only held there very briefly. Attention picks out the one phone number you care about, and that selection moves it into short-term memory, while the rest of the directory is not carried forward. Repeating the number, which is maintenance rehearsal, keeps it available long enough to dial. If it is rehearsed enough it can become represented in long-term memory, so you no longer need the directory in view. Later you can retrieve it from long-term memory back into short-term memory to dial it, which shows that the flow goes both ways and is not only a one-way trip toward long-term storage.

q: What are an icon and an echo, and what does persistence of vision show about sensory memory?
a: An icon is the fleeting visual trace left by stimulation, and an echo is the brief continuation of auditory information after a sound ends. They differ in modality, vision versus hearing, and they are not the durable representations used to remember something much later. Persistence of vision is the brief retention of the perception of light, and it is why a sparkler seems to leave a trail and why film frames feel continuous. It shows that sensory memory holds a lot of information for a short interval, which fills the gaps between moments of input, but its large capacity does not mean long duration, because the information decays quickly.
note: Film continuity is usually attributed to apparent motion (the phi phenomenon) and flicker fusion, not persistence of vision. Persistence of vision does account for the sparkler trail, and the icon is a brief stored trace, which is different from visible persistence.

q: What did Sperling (1960) do, and how do whole report, partial report and delayed partial report differ?
a: Sperling (1960) flashed an array of letters, three rows of four such as X M L T, A F N B, C D Z P, and asked what people had seen. The puzzle was whether people reported few letters because they only registered a few, or because the image faded before they could report everything. In whole report, participants report as many letters as they can. In partial report, a tone after the display tells them which row to report, so they cannot know in advance which row to memorize. In delayed partial report, the tone comes after an extra delay. The tone only comes after the display is gone, so strong partial report means information about all the rows was available at the start.

q: What were Sperling’s (1960) results, and what do they show about the capacity and duration of sensory memory?
a: In Sperling (1960), whole report averaged 4.5 of 12 letters, about 37.5 percent. Immediate partial report averaged 3.3 of 4 letters, about 82 percent, no matter which row was cued. Delayed partial report fell to about 1 of 4, or 25 percent, in the delayed-cue condition. Because people could report almost any cued row, far more than four or five letters must have been available at first, so the whole-report limit is a limit on reporting before the trace fades, not on what was perceived. Sensory memory therefore has a large capacity but fast decay, with most information lost within about one second unless it is selected for further processing. As the cue is delayed, partial-report accuracy drops toward the whole-report level, which links the advantage to a rapidly fading representation and does not support holding the whole array indefinitely.

q: What is memory span, and what is the traditional estimate for short-term memory?
a: Short-term memory holds small amounts briefly and is easily disrupted by interruption and interference. Memory span is the amount that can be recalled accurately in a task. The traditional estimate is seven plus or minus two units, but it depends on the kind of units and the task and should not be used for every visual-memory result.
note: Miller’s seven plus or minus two is about chunks, and modern estimates are nearer four chunks. The slides also give five to seven items elsewhere, so the two figures on the slides do not match each other.

q: How do recoding, maintenance rehearsal and elaborative rehearsal differ?
a: Recoding reorganizes or modifies information in short-term memory. Maintenance rehearsal repeats information to prolong its availability, like repeating a label. Elaborative rehearsal links new information with existing long-term knowledge, which supports longer-term learning. They are different control processes, because repeating a label is not the same as explaining how it relates to what you already know.

q: What does short-term memory do in current thought, what does Clive Wearing show, and how do duration and capacity differ?
a: Short-term memory includes selected sensory input and information retrieved from long-term memory, and it is what lets you understand a sentence, do arithmetic, dial a number or navigate. It acts as a window on the present, and this active availability differs from the large body of knowledge stored outside current awareness. Clive Wearing is a case of memory impairment. Keeping immediate information and remembering across events are different memory functions, so a case like his has to be analyzed function by function. Duration is how long information stays available and capacity is how much can be held. Rehearsal can extend duration and chunking can extend effective capacity, so a result can reflect the strategy used and not only the memory system.

q: Why did Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) have participants count backward by threes?
a: Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) presented three letters followed by a number, and participants counted backward by threes during a delay of 3 to 18 seconds and then recalled the letters. The counting prevents ordinary maintenance rehearsal, so participants cannot simply keep repeating the letters. Comparing the delays therefore measures retention when rehearsal is blocked.

q: What happened to recall after a long delay on the first trial versus many trials later in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959)?
a: In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), on the first trial recall was high at three seconds and still relatively high at eighteen seconds, because no earlier letters from the task competed with the current set. By the third trial recall at eighteen seconds was lower than on the first trial, since earlier sets now competed. After many trials recall at long delays was substantially reduced, because accumulated earlier material interfered with the set being tested. The same delay did far more damage when more earlier material had piled up, so trial history matters and the drop is not only the passage of eighteen seconds.
note: Brown and Peterson and Peterson found the decline in recall with delay. The trial-by-trial proactive-interference analysis is usually credited to Keppel and Underwood (1962), who are not named on the slides.

q: Why does the average over all trials give a misleading impression in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959)?
a: In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), the average over all trials makes it look like a steady loss with time, as though short-term memory simply decays. But the average mixes very different trials together. Early trials have high recall even at 18 seconds, and later trials have very low recall at 18 seconds. The steep drop comes mostly from the later trials, where proactive interference is strongest, so averaging hides interference behind something that looks like decay. Decay is loss associated with the passage of time, and proactive interference is when earlier information disrupts remembering newer information. Because earlier trials affect later recall, the Brown–Peterson pattern is evidence for interference and challenges treating every loss as pure time-based decay. The effective duration is about 15 to 20 seconds, and rehearsal and interference conditions affect the outcome.
note: The slides say recall at 18 seconds is relatively high on the first trial and substantially reduced on later trials, and that the average is a decline from shorter to longer delays that combines early trials with little interference and later trials with more. The words steady and very low are stronger than the slides.

q: Which concept describes earlier trigrams making new letters harder to recall in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959)?
a: It is proactive interference, which occurs when earlier information disrupts remembering newer information. In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), earlier trials affect later recall, because the trigrams from earlier trials compete with the one being tested, so the loss is not explained solely by elapsed time.

q: How does retroactive interference differ from proactive interference, and what is an example of each?
a: The direction of the competition is what differs. Retroactive interference is when new information disrupts memory for older information, so the affected memory is the old one and the interfering information arrived later. Learning a new phone number making the old number harder to retrieve is the example. Proactive interference is when old information disrupts memory for newer information, such as previous parking locations interfering with remembering where you parked today. Routine events are especially vulnerable because similar memories compete, and both types can be reduced when events are distinctive. To label it correctly, first decide which information is being recalled, then ask whether the competitor came earlier or later.

q: What is digit span, and how is it scored?
a: Digit span is the longest sequence of digits recalled correctly in order. The lists get longer, from four items to ten, and the longest list reproduced completely and in order defines the span. Getting the digits right but out of order does not count, one successful short list does not establish the limit, and one missed digit makes a longer list incorrect. Capacity differs between individuals and can be affected by strategies.

q: What did Miller (1956) propose, and how do Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) change the picture?
a: Miller (1956), in The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two, proposed that short-term capacity is about seven units, where the unit can differ across tasks, such as digits, words, numbers or phrases. The title is not proof that every short-term system holds exactly seven raw sensory elements. A unit can hold different amounts of information, so Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) compared colored squares with more complex objects using change detection. Their alternative emphasis is on the amount or complexity of information, not a fixed number of equally sized items.

q: How does the change-detection task of Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) work, and what did it show about visual short-term memory capacity?
a: Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) used change detection to measure visual short-term memory, VSTM, by comparing displays after a delay. Participants briefly view a first array, S1, for 100 milliseconds, and it then disappears, so they must keep the relevant visual properties in memory. A second display, S2, appears for 2,000 milliseconds and they judge whether it is the same or different. Correct answers require comparing S2 with the remembered S1, not looking at two arrays at once. Accuracy falls sharply when the set size goes above roughly four items, giving a capacity of about three to four items in visual working memory. That differs from the seven-plus-or-minus-two estimate for other tasks, and different tasks do not have to measure one identical capacity.

q: How does stimulus complexity affect visual capacity in Alvarez and Cavanagh’s (2004) work?
a: In Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004), same–different performance depends on how complex the stimuli are. Colored squares support a higher estimated capacity than more complex polygons or shaded cubes, and Chinese-character-like forms were also compared. Treating every stimulus as an equally sized item hides these differences, because capacity is constrained by the amount of information needed to represent the objects. Familiarity and the structure given to a stimulus can also change what counts as a unit of information. So a capacity for one category of stimulus is not a universal estimate for all visual objects.

q: What is chunking, and what did Ericsson and colleagues (1980) show?
a: Chunking combines smaller units into larger meaningful units. Ericsson and colleagues (1980) trained a student to reach a digit span of 79 by using familiar running times to organize the digits. The gain depends on knowledge-based organization, not on expanding every raw memory limit equally.

q: What did Chase and Simon (1973) find about chess recall, and what do control processes lead to?
a: In Chase and Simon (1973), chess masters recall more correct piece placements than beginners for meaningful game positions, but the advantage is greatly reduced for random arrangements. The experts’ edge comes from chunks that represent familiar relationships among pieces, and randomizing those relationships removes most of the benefit even though the pieces are the same kinds. Control processes include rehearsal, strategies for making material memorable such as the memory palace, and directing attention, and considering these active operations leads toward working memory, which concerns using and managing currently available information.
